I am 63 years old, and I have farmed these fields in Quzhou County since I was a young man. I only finished primary school, but I know this land and this climate. On the North China Plain, there is only one sensible way to use my 7 mu of good flat land: the winter wheat–summer maize double crop that every household around here plants. I do not gamble with new crops like stevia or cotton at my age; wheat and maize have steady buyers and the government gives us a grain subsidy.

For winter wheat, I sow improved varieties such as Jimai 22 in early October, right after the National Day holiday. I rotary till the soil first to break up the stubble. As basal fertilizer I spread about 100 jin of compound fertilizer per mu, and at green-up I topdress with urea. All together that gives the crop roughly 18 kg of nitrogen, 11 kg of phosphorus, and 4 kg of potassium per mu. I irrigate three times: once before winter so the seedlings survive the cold, once at jointing in spring, and once at heading when the ears are filling. I spray herbicide once, insecticide twice for aphids and armyworm, and fungicide once if the weather turns humid. If the year is normal I expect about 500 kg per mu.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I immediately plant hybrid maize—Denghai 605 or something similar from the seed dealer—without tilling, because there is no time to waste in the short summer season. I put down compound fertilizer at sowing, about 80 jin per mu, which gives around 11 kg nitrogen, 3 kg phosphorus, and 3 kg potassium per mu. Maize needs less fertilizer than wheat. I irrigate twice, at the jointing stage and again at grain filling. I spray herbicide once and insecticide twice for corn borer. With decent rain and sun, I expect about 550 kg per mu. Then the straw goes back to the field, and I prepare for wheat again.
